sources.title: Art B. Owen, Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples, Chapter 9: Importance Sampling
sources.locator: §9.1, printed pp. 3–5 (PDF pp. 3–5), including Theorem 9.1 and equations (9.2)–(9.4); §9.2, printed pp. 8–9, on unknown normalizing constants.

contents.name: §9.1, support condition, weighted sample mean, and Theorem 9.1 variance formula

source_review.read_extent: Read §9.1 from the finite-sample estimator through the proof of Theorem 9.1, including the support condition and weighted second-moment formula.
source_review.supports: The scaled formal importance-sampling variable and its finite-sample variance identity used by the local change-of-measure proof.
source_review.limitations: The chapter assumes the normalized target/proposal ratio can be computed. The local theorem does not pass an unknown partition constant to that algorithm.

contents.name: §9.2, self-normalized importance sampling with unknown normalizing constants

source_review.read_extent: Read the equations defining the self-normalized ratio estimate and the preceding discussion distinguishing it from ordinary importance sampling.
source_review.supports: The explicit warning that unknown normalizers require a ratio estimate rather than ordinary importance sampling.
source_review.limitations: The local finite raw-weight ratio theorem is proved separately and is exactly unbiased; the source treats self-normalized expectation estimates.

sources.title: Art B. Owen, Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples, Chapter 10: Advanced Variance Reduction
sources.locator: §10.9, printed pp. 39–45 (PDF pp. 39–45), bridge, umbrella, and path sampling, including the intermediate-distribution product identity.

contents.name: §10.9, path sampling through intermediate normalized distributions

source_review.read_extent: Read §10.9 through the finite path identity (10.48), including the intermediate normalized distributions and the product of stage ratio estimates.
source_review.supports: The use of intermediate distributions to factor a normalizing-constant ratio and the need to distinguish path estimates from a single poor-overlap step.
source_review.limitations: The source formula is a bridge/path-sampling ratio-of-expectations method; the local algorithm is the simpler product of independent raw-ratio means and is proved separately.

contents.name: §10.9, distinction between bridge estimators and the unbiased one-sided importance estimate

source_review.read_extent: Read the discussion of the one-sided estimate (10.38), bridge sampling (10.39), and the path product (10.48).
source_review.supports: The methodological distinction between an unbiased one-sided ratio estimate and bridge/path ratio estimators.
source_review.limitations: No exact variance formula for the local independent finite product is imported; its proof uses the local one-stage theorem and stage independence.

sources.title: Xiao-Li Meng and Wing Hung Wong, Simulating Ratios of Normalizing Constants via a Simple Identity: A Theoretical Exploration
sources.locator: §1, printed pp. 831–834 (PDF pp. 1–3); §2, printed pp. 834–835 (PDF pp. 3–4); §3, printed pp. 835–837 (PDF pp. 4–6).

contents.name: §§1–2, common-support normalizing-constant ratio identity and estimator

source_review.read_extent: Read the finite support setup in §1 and the full derivation of identity (2.3) in §2.
source_review.supports: The independent literature formulation of normalizing-constant ratios and the importance of support overlap.
source_review.limitations: The paper’s main estimator is a ratio of two sample means; the local one-sided raw-ratio estimator and exact finite variance are proved independently.

contents.name: §3, independent-draw relative mean-square analysis for the bridge ratio estimator

source_review.read_extent: Read the opening assumptions, relative-error definition, independent-sample hypothesis, and first-order variance calculation in §3.
source_review.supports: The requirement to state sample independence and distinguish exact finite variance from asymptotic ratio-estimator variance.
source_review.limitations: The paper explicitly uses a first-order approximation for a ratio estimator; that approximation is not used in the exact finite proof here.

contents.name: §§2–3, overlap and finite product-law example context

source_review.read_extent: Read the overlap condition in §2 and the independent-sampling error analysis in §3.
source_review.supports: The role of distributional overlap in importance-ratio variance.
source_review.limitations: The exact product chi-square factorization and exponential sample-size implication are derived locally.

sources.title: R. B. Kearfott, Interval Computations: Introduction, Uses, and Resources
sources.locator: §1, printed pp. 95–97 (PDF pp. 1–3): exact interval operation ranges, endpoint formulas, composition, and directed rounding.

contents.name: §1, exact interval images of addition, subtraction, multiplication and division

source_review.read_extent: Read §1, equations (1)–(6), and the directed-rounding discussion through its explanation of composed interval computations.
source_review.supports: The interval operation semantics used by the finite-sum and weighted-sum procedure.
source_review.limitations: The procedure’s finite-DAG output claims are supported by the exact imported interval lemma and are proved in the local theorem.

source_review.read_extent: Read §1 paragraphs on outward rounding and rigorous enclosures for composed operations.
source_review.supports: The context for enclosing a finite arithmetic expression with outward operations.
source_review.limitations: The complete induction for this precise input/output contract is given locally and through its exact imported mathematical supplier.

sources.title: Warwick Tucker, Validated Numerics: A Short Introduction to Rigorous Computations
sources.locator: Chapter 1 §§1.3–1.5, printed pp. 5–18 (PDF pp. 6–19); the retrieved publisher excerpt contains the complete cited chapter.

contents.name: Chapter 1 §1.3, exact directed rounding down and up

source_review.read_extent: Read the complete §1.3 definition of directed rounding and its endpoint bracketing properties.
source_review.supports: The conversion of rational input endpoints into enclosing finite dyadic endpoints.
source_review.limitations: The excerpt is Chapter 1 of the book and does not supply interval-DAG soundness; the separate interval definition/lemma and local proof do that.

contents.name: Chapter 1 §1.6.3, finite summation by directed rounding

source_review.read_extent: Read the complete finite partial-sum example and its upper/lower enclosure argument.
source_review.supports: A finite computation can return outward lower and upper bounds for an exact sum.
source_review.limitations: This example’s tail estimate and floating-point arithmetic are not used as premises; the local result proves the finite DAG statement.
